analysis.one_liner: Protects insurers from federal penalties for covering state-legal cannabis businesses.
analysis.headline: Sens. Kevin Cramer and Ruben Gallego introduced the bill with one cosponsor, and it has sat in the Senate Banking Committee since July 2026 without a hearing or vote, with the session ending in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: In the roughly 40 states where cannabis is legal under state law, insurers have generally avoided covering cannabis businesses because the product is still illegal under federal law and insurers fear federal penalties. This bill bars federal agencies from penalizing insurers, or canceling their other business, because they insure a state-legal cannabis business, its workers, or landlords who lease to it. It also shields insurers and their employees from federal liability solely for doing that business, and orders a GAO study of barriers facing minority-owned and women-owned cannabis businesses. It does not require any insurer to cover cannabis businesses and does not change federal cannabis prohibition.
analysis.who_benefits: State-legal cannabis businesses — growers, processors, dispensaries — that currently struggle to find insurers willing to write property, casualty, and liability coverage; their employees, who can lose out on workplace coverage; tribal cannabis enterprises; and landlords and equipment lessors who lease to cannabis businesses and can see their own policies dropped. Insurers also gain access to a new market without federal liability risk.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Legal cannabis businesses, their workers, and insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars federal agencies from prohibiting, penalizing, or discouraging insurers from writing coverage for state-legal cannabis businesses, and from terminating or limiting an insurer's other policies solely because it serves such businesses.

It protects an insurer and its officers, directors, and employees from liability under any federal law or regulation solely for engaging in the business of insurance with a cannabis-related legitimate business, or for reinvesting income from that business.

It also bars adverse federal action against policies held by cannabis business owners and employees, and by owners of real estate or equipment leased to cannabis businesses, solely because of that connection.

It directs the Comptroller General (GAO) to study and report on barriers to marketplace entry and access to financial services for minority-owned and women-owned cannabis businesses, with recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear only the cost of the GAO study. No insurer is required to cover cannabis businesses, and the bill preserves state insurance regulation under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, so there is no direct cost shifted to the public. The main limit falls on cannabis businesses themselves: the bill leaves federal prohibition in place and does not extend safe-harbor protections to banks or payment processors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Essentially no one; limits fall on cannabis businesses

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor covers only insurers. Although the bill's definitions of "financial service" include payment processing, money transmission, and armored car services, the operative protections in the bill apply only to insurers, so cannabis businesses remain largely cut off from banks and still operate heavily in cash.
No insurer is required to serve cannabis businesses, so coverage may not become available even with legal protection in place; the bill preserves insurers' discretion and state insurance regulation.

The bill does not change federal cannabis prohibition itself, so the underlying conflict between state-legal markets and federal law remains, and the GAO study produces findings and recommendations but requires no follow-up action.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, well-scoped fix rather than a large transfer either way. The direct cost to the public is essentially zero, and it could reduce real harm: cannabis businesses in legal states operate uninsured or underinsured, which puts employees, landlords, and even neighboring businesses at risk when fires, thefts, or accidents occur. The honest objection is that it is a partial remedy: without banking protections or a change in federal prohibition, cannabis businesses stay cash-heavy, and insurance may remain thin because insurers are invited, not required, to enter the market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late July 2026 and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which has taken no action on it, and with the session ending in early January 2027 it is likely to run out of time without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Kevin Cramer introduced S. 5049, the CLAIM Act, on July 21, 2026, for himself and Sen. Ruben Gallego.
The bill's only cosponsor is a Democrat, giving it a bipartisan pair of sponsors from the start.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost anything concrete yet, since the bill has not moved: the status quo persists, with state-legal cannabis businesses still unable to reliably obtain insurance and the current prohibition-era boundaries intact for insurers, banks, and federal agencies.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is bipartisan — a Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor — and no opposing votes or public opposition appear in the record, because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill opens a new market of state-legal cannabis clients and shields insurers and their staff from federal liability for serving them. Its benefit to the public comes through insurance availability for a largely uninsured business sector, though insurers are not required to enter that market.

industries.industry: State-legal cannabis businesses and their workers
industries.note: Cannabis growers, processors, dispensaries, and their employees currently face difficulty obtaining property, liability, and related coverage; the safe harbor makes it possible for insurers to cover them without federal penalty. It also extends protection to landlords and equipment lessors serving the industry, and includes tribal cannabis operations.

The bill defines financial services broadly enough to include payment processing, money transmission, and armored car services, but its operative safe harbor protects only insurers, so banks and payment companies gain little from this bill and remain exposed under current federal guidance.

analysis.trajectory: With the session ending in early January 2027 and no committee action since the July referral, the bill is likely to die without a vote unless the Banking Committee schedules it in the remaining weeks. Comparable cannabis financial-services bills have historically stalled in this committee even with broad support, so a floor vote before adjournment would be unusual.
